definition: In machine learning, a neural scaling law is an empirical scaling law that describes how neural network performance changes as key factors are scaled up or down.
details: These factors typically include the number of parameters, training dataset size, and training cost. Some models also exhibit performance gains by scaling inference through increased test-time compute (TTC), extending neural scaling laws beyond training to the deployment phase.

explainer.lead: Neural scaling laws are empirical descriptions of how network performance changes as parameters, data or training cost are scaled. They matter because they let teams predict gains before spending large compute budgets.

tiers.eli5: It's a rule of thumb that says roughly how much better the model gets when you give it more data, more size, or more training.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use them to plan compute and data budgets, and increasingly to weigh extra test-time compute at deployment. A pitfall is treating them as guaranteed, since they are empirical and model-specific.
tiers.paperLevel: A neural scaling law is an empirical law describing how performance changes as factors such as number of parameters, training dataset size and training cost scale up or down; some models also gain from scaling test-time compute (TTC) at deployment.

explainer.example: A team observes that increasing parameters and dataset size together improves performance along a predictable trend, and uses that trend to choose a training budget.
